beats.trigger: You can't tell if your agent is safe from its output.
beats.got: I need a repeatable check, not a gut feel about the output.

beats.trigger: Prework covers personal skills and agent risk layered on normal security.
beats.got: nothing new, a reading list I probably haven't done

beats.trigger: **Evaluate** residual risk: what is left, and what future sessions need before touching the system
beats.got: The module ends with me writing down what risk is left, which is useful for the pricing work.

beats.trigger: Name what you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: Frame it as my CFO and working group seeing the output, so I'd list source trust and customer data.

beats.trigger: A tool call is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: The agent writes text, the harness runs it as an action, so a vague tool description gives a bad action.

beats.trigger: Would you bet your job on it being safe?
beats.got: The unease about my pricing agent doesn't go away with a policy tick-box.

beats.trigger: That is why perimeter, access control and patching work.
beats.got: nothing new, I know classic security assumes predictable software

beats.trigger: The attack surface is the instruction set.
beats.got: A document my agent reads can talk it into acting, and my pricing sources are documents.

beats.trigger: Scope (give the agent less). Split (two agents, different trust levels). Filter (post-process output). Gate (human approves). Review (a second agent judges).
beats.got: Five concrete mitigation moves I can name to my team.

beats.trigger: **"I can't tell"** is a real answer. Closing it takes evidence, not a better guess.
beats.got: I can say "unknown" in a report and that's legitimate, which is how a CFO review actually works.

beats.trigger: More context makes a good answer likelier. Less access makes a bad answer smaller.
beats.got: Cutting access limits how bad a wrong answer gets, and I'd sign for that tradeoff.

beats.trigger: Every door you don't open is a residual risk you don't have to name, mitigate or re-test.
beats.got: Mostly the same point as the previous slide, said again in different words.

beats.trigger: Damn, this is complex stuff.
beats.got: nothing new, a pep-talk restating the loop; the swearing felt oddly performed

beats.trigger: a skill is a reusable check you run again instead of re-prompting from memory.

beats.trigger: Read the first few rows: they show which rules files can check and which need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.

beats.trigger: Push back on anything that sounds like a generic GDPR brochure.

beats.trigger: Expect many questions; the agent keeps probing both lenses over several rounds.

beats.trigger: "You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."

beats.trigger: The uncomfortable feeling is the evidence.

beats.trigger: The risk remains. That is expected. Name it, accept it on record, and stop there.

take_homes: Run the two-lens audit (company policy plus what the agent can reach and be misled by) on the pricing-pilot agent before it goes near the working group.
Name the leftover risk in writing and accept it on record, including 'I can't tell' rows, instead of claiming the agent is safe.
Smallest mitigation first: scope down access, add a human gate, and take unclear rows to legal or security with a narrow question.

monday.move: Run the saved /agent-audit check on the usage-pricing brief agent, apply one mitigation (human gate on anything leaving the team), and write the residual into the report
monday.who: Me, then walk two of my fourteen through the report
monday.when: Monday morning before the pricing working group meeting
monday.stop_condition: One mitigation applied and the residual risk written down, even if rows are still 'can't tell'
monday.blocker: No shared place for the skill and context files, so my team would each get their own copy

misconception.why: I built the skill by dictating what matters and answering the interview, which is closer to 'writing a check' than 'writing better prompts'. But I still see it as prompt skill, just applied to a checker; nothing directly challenged it.

one_line: The audit loop is the useful part and it found things I hadn't seen; the lecture says the same point four times and the module leaves my team with no shared place for the skill.
